health.physical: Gabriel has chronic lumbar pain and reduced tolerance for prolonged standing, bending, and lifting following years of physically demanding maintenance work and a later back injury. He can walk, and he deliberately maintains regular low-impact activity, but he paces himself and uses familiar flat routes. He follows a home physical-therapy routine when symptoms permit and takes prescribed medication. He tries to keep preventive and follow-up appointments, although transportation, paperwork, and irregular sleep can make scheduling difficult.
health.mental_and_emotional: He continues to grieve his wife and has periods of loneliness, worry, and low motivation. He has spoken with a counselor and is open to using support when it feels practical and respectful. He is not defined by a diagnosis and does not present as continually distressed; he can be humorous and engaged, while still having difficult nights and anniversaries. He does not report an active crisis or current intent to harm himself.
health.health_habits: He prioritizes wellbeing when practical: regular walking, physical-therapy movements, medication, and keeping medical appointments are meaningful efforts for him. His health habits are imperfect rather than all-or-nothing. Sleep is often insufficient because he stays up late, and he snacks frequently, including cookies, but he tries to make ordinary meals that do not aggravate his health.
health.access_and_stress: Healthcare affordability is a major public concern for him, and medical bills or unclear coverage rules cause anxiety. His low income makes budgeting and continuity of care important. He uses eligible public coverage and appreciates concrete assistance, even though he does not believe government should be responsible for providing healthcare generally.

relationships.name: Elena Sandoval
relationships.description: Gabriel's wife, who died in 2022 after an illness. He still thinks of her as his closest companion and sometimes speaks about her in the present tense before correcting himself. Their shared life and her death remain central to how he understands the financial and emotional changes of the past several years.

relationships.name: Teresa Sandoval
relationships.description: His mother, who lives elsewhere in the Sacramento area. She is an important source of family continuity and practical support. Gabriel checks on her and sometimes helps with small errands, while trying not to let either of them feel that every visit has to be about his difficulties.

relationships.name: Andre Sandoval
relationships.description: His older brother, with whom he has a straightforward, occasionally teasing relationship. They can disagree about politics without cutting off contact. Andre is one of the few people Gabriel would call if an urgent practical problem arose.

relationships.name: Maya
relationships.description: His niece, whom he cares about and encourages without trying to supervise every decision. He sometimes sends her a short message about school, work, or a family event, and is pleased when she asks him about their relatives' history.

relationships.name: Darnell
relationships.description: A former coworker from the hotel maintenance team. They exchange occasional texts about old colleagues, Sacramento traffic, and practical repairs. Darnell understands that Gabriel is no longer able to work as he once did and does not pressure him to return.

relationships.name: Rosa
relationships.description: A neighbor in his apartment building who has become a familiar, low-pressure friend. They trade small favors and check that the other has received important building notices. Gabriel enjoys talking with her in passing but does not depend on her as a caregiver.

relationships.name: Dr. Patel and his clinic team
relationships.description: A primary-care team that helps him manage back pain, prescriptions, and follow-up care. Gabriel appreciates clear explanations and is more likely to speak openly when he feels his concerns have been heard rather than dismissed.

other_facts: Gabriel was born in California and has lived in the Sacramento region for most of his life.
He identifies as multiracial, with Mexican-American roots on his mother's side and African-American roots on his father's side.
He does not treat either branch of his family as a decorative label; the people and stories matter more to him than a simplified account of identity.
He grew up around relatives who practiced Catholicism, but he is now unaffiliated and does not believe he needs a religious label to have a moral life.
Some family gatherings still take place around religious holidays, and he attends when the purpose is to see relatives rather than to affirm a faith he does not hold.
He can recognize familiar Spanish expressions from family life and uses a few, but he is not fluent and does not pretend otherwise.
As a teenager, he liked taking apart broken household items to see how they worked, even though he was not especially interested in formal science classes.
He entered community college with a practical goal and completed training that helped him get maintenance work.
His bachelor's degree came later, through part-time study while he was working; it was a personal achievement but did not replace the value of hands-on experience for him.
He was proud when he finished his degree, though he rarely brings it up unless someone asks about his education.
He worked several evening shifts in hotel maintenance and became accustomed to dealing with unexpected problems after most office staff had gone home.
He was known for noticing a loose hinge, a leaking fixture, or a failing piece of equipment before a guest complaint made the problem urgent.
He learned to distinguish a quick safe repair from a job that needed a licensed tradesperson, and he is more cautious about that distinction now than he was in his twenties.
His wife Elena's illness changed the couple's financial plans and daily routines before her death.
The period after Elena died included grief, reduced household income, and the loss of stable housing; he now has an apartment but still remembers how precarious that period felt.
His household consists of him alone. His annual household income is approximately $18,600, primarily from disability income, placing it below $25,000.
He is not currently in the labor force and is not actively seeking employment; this is not a temporary choice to take a vacation or a claim that he has no useful skills.
He has no children and sometimes wonders what his life would look like if he and Elena had made different plans, but he does not treat that uncertainty as a regret he needs to resolve.
He keeps a small number of Elena's belongings in ordinary use rather than placing everything in storage; familiar objects feel more comforting than a formal memorial display.
He once tried to force himself to attend a large community event after Elena's death and left early. Since then, he has accepted that smaller visits are a better fit.
His current apartment is modest, and he prioritizes keeping the rent paid, having working appliances, and maintaining a clear path through the rooms over decorating.
He has experienced unstable housing but is not currently without a home; the subsidized apartment is an important source of safety and routine.

He is careful about accepting favors because he worries that an offer may create an obligation he cannot repay. With trusted relatives, he is slowly learning that help can be mutual without being a debt.
He sometimes buys a familiar brand even when a cheaper option exists, then adjusts elsewhere in the month rather than feeling pleased about having saved a few dollars on something he uses daily.
He does not own a pet and does not seek one out; he recognizes that caring for an animal would add responsibility he is not sure his health and budget could support.
He has no strong interest in owning a car and is accustomed to planning local errands around buses, walking, and occasional rides from relatives.
He enjoys hearing older relatives tell the same family story more than once, because each retelling tends to include a detail that was missing before.
He keeps some family photographs on his phone and occasionally sends one to his brother or niece with a short note about who is pictured.
He is protective of his privacy on unfamiliar websites and dislikes being asked for more personal information than seems necessary to complete a task.
He is active on social media but does not assume that a frequent online presence means he wants a constant flow of direct messages.
He sometimes shares a news link without much commentary, then becomes more engaged if someone asks him what he thinks rather than immediately arguing.
His conservative views and unaffiliated status coexist with close relationships across a range of beliefs; he prefers particular conversations with people he knows over broad political performance.

He thinks the economy is doing excellently in broad terms even though his own family's finances are worse than four years ago; in his mind, national indicators and household experience answer different questions.
He notices higher grocery and service prices but reports no inflation-related hardship because his current hardship is more directly tied to disability, bereavement, and limited income.

He worries about healthcare affordability for the country even while opposing the idea that government should generally provide healthcare, and he accepts targeted assistance when it is available to him.
He supports specific gun-safety measures while also believing that responsible adults should retain the right to own firearms; he does not regard those positions as mutually exclusive.
He considers democracy very threatened and worries about post-election violence, but he still values local institutions and ordinary civic participation.
He disapproves of the Supreme Court while believing that the institution itself should remain; his criticism is directed at its decisions and perceived distance from ordinary people.
He rarely travels overnight and has no ambition to collect destinations. A familiar meal with his family in Sacramento is more appealing than an elaborate trip.
He is most likely to enjoy an outing if there is a clear reason to go, a place to sit, a manageable cost, and an easy way to return home.
He sometimes feels that people mistake his resistance to new products for a lack of curiosity; he is interested in ideas, but wants evidence that a change will solve a real problem.
He has a small emergency cash reserve that he tries not to touch, even when he is tempted to make a purchase that would make a difficult week feel better.
He considers keeping an appointment, returning a call, and telling the truth about what he can manage to be more meaningful signs of character than grand promises.
He is still learning that a quieter life after loss can be a real life, rather than merely an unfinished version of the one he had with Elena.
